Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-15
Start time: 14:30 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes
Meeting id: ff-20261015-veridian-001
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Park (Redwood SE), Anika Rao (Veridian ML), Tom Easton (Veridian Platform), Jenna Li (Veridian SRE)

Summary (auto): quick review of last week's microburst results; decide kernel prioritization for TTFT and streaming; plan seq-len sweep in staging; agree next steps for on-prem capacity test and pricing.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining — hope you're all good. we have about 45 minutes, i think. quick roll call?
[00:08] Anika: hi, anika here. ready.
[00:10] Tom: tom, yep.
[00:12] Jenna: jenna, SRE.
[00:14] Diego: diego on the infra side.
[00:16] Maya: cool. quick agenda: diego will walk through kernel traces, we review the TTFT numbers from the microburst run, then decision on seq-len prioritization and next steps for on-prem.
[00:26] Diego: alright i'll share screen — i'm going to paraphrase the NVTX traces we captured on the 10-11 run. first call out: we saw two hotspots in attention compute for seqlen 256, and the streaming handshake added about 12ms on average for the TTF-T — sorry TTFT — first token path, when the KV cache wasn't warmed.
[00:51] Anika: can you repeat warm? the cache warm vs cold distinction — our typical traffic pattern is a lot of cold starts, since customers hit different patient records.
[01:02] Diego: yeah totally. cold means we don't have prefix cached so the model goes through full KV build. warm means subsequent requests reuse cached KV. cold starts were ~85ms median for first-token at 256-seq, warm were ~23ms.
[01:18] Tom: those 85ms are aggressive for us — with our UI SLAs we need <70ms 95th for first token, otherwise it feels laggy in the clinician flow.
[01:28] Maya: right — our aim here is to hit that 95th <70ms with reasonable cost. diego, what did kernel selection look like? any alternate kernels that help cold TTFT?
[01:38] Diego: we tried two paths: the fused attention kernel (we call it fast-attn-v2) and the fallback matmul path. fast-attn-v2 gives ~18% faster attention on avg at 128 and 64 sequence lengths, but it falls back on 256 for certain kv memory layouts on older GPUs. the matmul path was slower on mid-range cards but more predictable.
[02:03] Jenna: older GPUs — can you remind which we tested? our staging runs on A10s right now, production will be a mix incl some V100 in private hosts for regulatory zones.
[02:13] Diego: tests were on A10 and Ampere 80GB — but we also grabbed small samples on V100 to see fallback behavior. the V100s showed the fast-attn kernel falling back and latency spiking for seqlen 256.
[02:27] Anika: ok makes sense. for Veridian's workload, most prompts average ~110 tokens, with some rare longer sessions up to 600. 95% are <200.
[02:38] Maya: that's useful. so defaulting to optimize around 128 seems logical unless we see quality regressions.
[02:44] Tom: question: what about streaming overhead? we saw earlier that the handshake and chunked responses add overhead. can we reduce chunk size or adjust chunking policy?
[02:53] Diego: short answer: yes. we can tune chunk sizes and the streaming buffer flush cadence. for our infra we have two knobs — chunk size and early-flush threshold. lowering chunk size reduces jitter but increases per-request overhead.
[03:07] Anika: what's the net effect on TTFT for a 64-token chunk vs 256-token chunk?
[03:13] Diego: empirically in these runs, 64-token chunking shaved 6-9ms from the first-byte time in warm paths by starting earlier, but in cold paths the benefit was smaller because the KV build dominated.
[03:24] Jenna: so for cold-heavy traffic, chunking changes less; sequence length and kernel choice are bigger levers.
[03:30] Maya: ok let's walk decision tree. given Veridian's distribution (95% <200), diego recommends optimizing kernels for 128-seq. is that right?
[03:40] Diego: yes. pick fast-attn-v2 as default for A10/Ampere and use a kernel-hedging policy for V100 zones: we can monitor NVTX and if a path is slow, fallback to matmul. hedging would add a minor compute delta but reduces tail.
[03:55] Tom: hedging worries me because of cost spikes. can you estimate the cost delta? even a 5-8% bump month-on-month matters.
[04:04] Maya: i have a quick pricing sketch — i'll send a delta later today, but hedging cost depends on how often we hit the fallback. diego, what's the fallback frequency in our sample?
[04:12] Diego: in the 10-11 dataset, fallback frequency on V100 was ~22% for seqlen 256, but for 128 it was only ~4%. so if we move default to 128, hedging rarely triggers.
[04:25] Anika: that seems acceptable. the bigger risk is quality — do shorter seq lengths change outputs? we've seen truncation in some system prompts previously.
[04:33] Diego: model output quality is mostly preserved up to 128 for your prompt-set; however, if you have chains that rely on long context (>300) we need to pin those requests to a dedicated route with seqlen=512 and reserved capacity.
[04:47] Tom: we do have a small subset of long consults, maybe 2% of traffic which are long. can we route them to Dedicated?
[04:54] Maya: yes — this is a classic split: default hosted endpoints optimized for 128 seqlen, and reserved/dedicated pools for long sessions. that gives you tail predictability.
[05:04] Jenna: on security side, if those go to Dedicated in a private VPC, we also need KMS integration and audit logs. that won't change latency but affects deployment timeline.
[05:14] Maya: noted. diego, can you talk through the microburst numbers? you mentioned microburst traces earlier.
[05:20] Diego: sure. microbursts were simulated as 400 concurrent short requests over 10s window. key takeaway: for streaming-first token (TTFT) we saw a 2.4x variance in 95th across kernel choices for seqlen 256, and a 1.3x variance at 128. cold path amplifies this. the NVTX trace shows attention kernels blocked on shared memory at times, causing small stalls.
[05:47] Anika: 2.4x is big. where is the contention coming from — memory bandwidth, PCIe, or scheduler queuing?
[05:54] Diego: primarily shared memory and some warp-serialization — so kernel selection that uses warp-level reductions more efficiently helps. also batch scheduling: we saw that continuous batching policies reduced variance by smoothing microburst bursts, but that adds average latency if the batch window is too big.
[06:10] Maya: so another tradeoff: batching window size for throughput vs TTFT SLO. what's the recommended window for your microburst pattern?
[06:17] Diego: for your pattern i'd recommend a 6-10ms continuous batching window with adaptive thresholding: small window keeps TTFT low, but if load spikes we temporarily allow a slightly larger batch to protect throughput.
[06:28] Tom: can that be per-route? we have different UI endpoints with different SLOs.
[06:31] Diego: yes, per-route adaptive batching is supported.
[06:33] Anika: nice. about the seqlen sweep that maya asked us to run — what are the exact configs you want veridian to test?
[06:39] Diego: please run seqlen fixed runs at 64, 128, 256 with microburst pattern and steady-state pattern. measure TTFT median & 95th, CPU/GPU utilization, and kernel fallback counts. dump NVTX ranges or attach the profiling zip to the sheet.
[06:52] Anika: we'll do that. we'll likely run in staging on A10 and one on V100 to see differences.
[06:57] Maya: Diego, you mentioned a kernel mapping doc and a quick script to extract fallback counts — can you drop both into the shared folder? link is the poc sheet: https://redwood.app/drive/Veridian-POC-benchmarks (note: internal link, access granted to the team)
[07:12] Diego: yup i'll drop the mapping + an nvprof extraction script by monday.
[07:16] Tom: on Dedicated vs Hosted: we need a throughput test in our private cluster — i want to see per-GPU microburst headroom before we commit to reserved capacity. can redwood help schedule a run with your infra team?
[07:28] Maya: yes, we can coordinate. i'll introduce you to the infra ops folks — propose a 2-hour slot to run sustained microburst + a short 10s high concurrency stress. tentative week of 10/27.
[07:38] Jenna: also want to log the network hop latency. in our on-prem env we have an internal firewall that adds ~1ms per request sometimes — that can matter.
[07:48] Diego: good call — include network loopback tests and record p99 network latency. that'll help us separate model vs network contributions.
[07:56] Anika: i noticed in the shared CSV the 95th for 128 was 47ms but for warm paths. what about cold-start 95th for 128?
[08:04] Diego: cold-start 95th for 128 was 82ms in that CSV. so the warm/cold delta is significant — caching or sticky sessions could help.
[08:14] Anika: sticky sessions might not be possible for us due to privacy routing; we can't store patient tokens in cache across tenants.
[08:21] Maya: in that case we should plan for mostly cold starts and configure routing and kernels accordingly. diego, any quantization/precision changes that impact TTFT? we experimented with int8 some weeks ago.
[08:31] Diego: int8 reduced memory bandwidth and sped up certain kernels but increased variance on attention for seqlen >200 due to numerical recovery paths. for your traffic i wouldn't push int8 as default, maybe int8 for the Dedicated long-session route where you can pin model instances.
[08:46] Tom: are there any model-variant quality differences we should watch for if we change seqlen defaults? e.g., hallucination rates or truncated token issues?
[08:53] Diego: we've run your eval prompts; at 128 there are 2% edge-case differences mostly in long-chain summarization tasks. i'd mark those prompts as canaries and monitor quality metrics in the console.
[09:05] Anika: that's doable. please add the canary prompt set to the shared repo.
[09:09] Diego: will do.
[09:11] Maya: quick pause — we are at 9 minutes into the call? no, actually 9 minutes marker in the recording; we've covered the big things. any blockers from veridian that stop us picking 128 default?
[09:22] Anika: none from ML side. we need the seq-sweep results to convince compliance that performance won't impact clinical flow.
[09:30] Tom: platform needs the Dedicated throughput numbers and the cost delta.
[09:34] Maya: ok next steps recap: diego share kernel mapping + script (due 10/19); anika run sweep (due 10/21) and attach results; maya share pricing delta for hedging vs non-hedging (due 10/18); schedule on-prem throughput test week of 10/27.
[09:50] Jenna: one more question: monitoring — do you expose token-level tracing and per-request NV metrics in the console? we need to tie regressions to requests.
[09:58] Diego: yes per-request traces with token time-breakdowns are available in Redwood Console; we'll enable the request-level debug retention for the POC so you can see token-level times. note this increases storage and cost, but for debugging it's helpful.
[10:12] Anika: please enable for two weeks.
[10:15] Maya: i'll toggle that and capture retention costs in the pricing doc.
[10:19] Tom: security question — audit logs for Dedicated: will they show kernel choices and fallback counts or only higher-level metrics?
[10:27] Diego: audit logs will contain route choices, model variant, and a summary of kernel fallback counts (aggregated). NVTX traces are downloadable but not in the audit log.
[10:38] Jenna: good. that's fine.
[10:40] Maya: any other items?
[10:42] Anika: none.
[10:44] Diego: one small note — we saw occasional misattribution in the profiler names where the service labeled an op 'atten' instead of 'attention' so be aware traces may have shorthand.
[10:54] Maya: okay thanks. we'll capture that in the README.
[10:58] Maya: recap of decisions: default to optimize for seqlen=128 in hosted routes; enable hedging for legacy V100 zones but low trigger; route long sessions (>300) to Dedicated; run seqlen sweep and on-prem throughput test.
[11:15] Tom: agreed.
[11:16] Anika: agreed.
[11:17] Jenna: agreed.
[11:18] Maya: excellent. i'll send meeting notes + action items. thanks all.
